differential: Kaposi Sarcoma
This malignancy is strongly associated with HIV and classically presents as asymptomatic, violaceous papules or nodules on the face.
Molluscum Contagiosum
Disseminated and persistent molluscum is a common opportunistic viral infection in HIV, presenting as asymptomatic, flesh-colored, umbilicated papules.
Cutaneous Cryptococcosis
This opportunistic fungal infection can disseminate to the skin in immunocompromised patients, often causing asymptomatic papules on the head and neck that can mimic molluscum.
Bacillary Angiomatosis
Caused by *Bartonella* species, this opportunistic infection presents with vascular papules and nodules in HIV patients that can resemble Kaposi sarcoma.
Secondary Syphilis
Known as "the great imitator," secondary syphilis can present with a variety of non-pruritic skin lesions and has a high rate of co-infection with HIV.
eliminated: Herpes Zoster
This diagnosis is unlikely due to the explicit denial of pain, a hallmark symptom.
Allergic Contact Dermatitis
The absence of pruritus makes this inflammatory condition highly improbable.

differential: Cryptococcosis
This opportunistic fungal infection is a primary consideration in an HIV patient presenting with umbilicated papules and lymphadenopathy, which can signify disseminated disease.
Molluscum contagiosum
This viral infection classically causes umbilicated papules and can be widespread and persistent in individuals with advanced HIV.
Histoplasmosis
Disseminated infection with this endemic fungus can manifest with umbilicated skin lesions, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy in immunocompromised patients.
Penicilliosis (Talaromycosis)
This opportunistic fungal infection, particularly in patients with exposure to Southeast Asia, is a classic cause of umbilicated papules and systemic illness in HIV.
Basal cell carcinoma
Although typically solitary and slow-growing, this common skin cancer can present as a papule with central umbilication and occurs with increased frequency in immunocompromised hosts.
eliminated: Kaposi sarcoma
Lesions are typically violaceous plaques or nodules, not skin-colored umbilicated papules.
Acne vulgaris
Lesion morphology is inconsistent as acne does not cause umbilicated papules.
Varicella
Lesions are vesicular, not papular with central umbilication, and are typically associated with fever and pruritus.

differential: Cryptococcosis
The patient's HIV status and presence of umbilicated papules are classic for cutaneous manifestations of disseminated cryptococcosis.
Molluscum contagiosum
This viral infection is the most common cause of umbilicated papules, which can be numerous and widespread in immunocompromised individuals.
Histoplasmosis
This systemic fungal infection can disseminate and cause umbilicated skin lesions in patients with HIV, mimicking cryptococcosis.
Penicilliosis (Talaromycosis)
This is an important opportunistic fungal infection in endemic areas that characteristically presents with umbilicated papules on the face and neck in HIV patients.
Atypical mycobacterial infection
Cutaneous infections with nontuberculous mycobacteria can present as papules and nodules, which may umbilicate, in patients with impaired immunity.
eliminated: Basal cell carcinoma
Unlikely to present as multiple lesions with a rapid onset of only two weeks.

differential: Molluscum contagiosum

The clinical presentation of umbilicated papules in an HIV patient combined with biopsy showing intracytoplasmic inclusions and electron microscopy confirming a poxvirus is pathognomonic for this diagnosis.
Monkeypox
This orthopoxvirus can cause umbilicated papules and lymphadenopathy, but the patient's lack of fever or other systemic symptoms makes it less likely.
Orf (Contagious Ecthyma)
This is a parapoxvirus infection that can cause umbilicated lesions, but it is typically acquired from livestock and presents as a solitary, more inflammatory lesion on the hands.
Milker's nodule
This parapoxvirus infection would be confirmed by electron microscopy, but it characteristically causes lesions on the hands of individuals handling cattle, not multiple facial papules.
Smallpox (Variola)
Although eradicated, this orthopoxvirus causes umbilicated pustules, but it is ruled out by the lack of severe systemic illness and known exposure.
eliminated: Cutaneous cryptococcosis
Biopsy and electron microscopy revealed a poxvirus, not the encapsulated yeast characteristic of Cryptococcus.
Disseminated histoplasmosis
Histopathology did not show the intracellular yeast forms of Histoplasma capsulatum.
Basal cell carcinoma
Histopathology did not show nests of malignant basaloid cells.

differential: Kaposi Sarcoma
This is a common AIDS-defining malignancy that classically presents as asymptomatic violaceous papules or nodules on the face and neck.
Cutaneous Cryptococcosis
This opportunistic fungal infection can present with asymptomatic, umbilicated papules on the face in patients with advanced HIV.
Molluscum Contagiosum
This viral infection is common in immunocompromised individuals and can cause numerous, widespread, asymptomatic papules on the face.
Bacillary Angiomatosis
This opportunistic bacterial infection causes vascular lesions that mimic Kaposi sarcoma and is a key consideration in patients with HIV.
Disseminated Histoplasmosis
This systemic fungal infection can manifest with varied cutaneous lesions, including papules and nodules on the face, in an immunocompromised host.
eliminated: Herpes Zoster
Ruled out by the absence of pain, which is a hallmark symptom.
Allergic Contact Dermatitis
Unlikely due to the complete absence of pruritus.
Urticaria
Inconsistent with the 2-week stable duration of lesions and lack of itch.

differential: Molluscum contagiosum
The patient has umbilicated vesicles, a classic presentation for this poxvirus infection, which is often widespread on the face in individuals with HIV.
Cutaneous cryptococcosis
This disseminated fungal infection is a key mimic of molluscum contagiosum in immunocompromised patients and can present with umbilicated skin lesions and lymphadenopathy.
Disseminated Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) infection
Atypical VZV in an HIV patient can present as umbilicated vesicles, and the facial/neck distribution with lymphadenopathy is consistent with this diagnosis.
Disseminated histoplasmosis
This opportunistic fungal infection can manifest with umbilicated cutaneous lesions in patients with advanced HIV.
Atypical Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) infection
Chronic or disseminated HSV can present with atypical umbilicated lesions rather than classic vesicles in severely immunocompromised hosts.
eliminated: Allergic contact dermatitis
This diagnosis is unlikely given the specific morphology of umbilicated vesicles and the reported absence of itching.

differential: Molluscum Contagiosum
The presence of multiple umbilicated (dimpled) vesicles on the face and neck is a classic presentation for this poxvirus infection in an HIV-positive individual.
Cryptococcosis (Cutaneous)
This opportunistic fungal infection can present with umbilicated skin lesions that mimic molluscum contagiosum in immunocompromised patients.
Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)
Atypical, centrally umbilicated vesicles can be a manifestation of chronic or disseminated herpetic infection in an immunocompromised host.
Histoplasmosis (Cutaneous)
Disseminated infection with this endemic fungus can cause umbilicated skin lesions, particularly in patients with HIV.
Talaromycosis (Penicilliosis)
This systemic mycosis, particularly in patients with exposure to Southeast Asia, classically presents with umbilicated skin papules on the face and trunk in HIV patients.
eliminated: Kaposi Sarcoma
The lesions are described as vesicles, not the typical violaceous papules, plaques, or nodules of Kaposi sarcoma.
Bacterial Folliculitis
The lesions are described as umbilicated vesicles, not the typical erythematous pustules centered on hair follicles.

differential: Molluscum contagiosum
This is the most common poxvirus infection in HIV patients, classically presenting with umbilicated papules and Henderson-Patterson intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.
Monkeypox (Mpox)
This orthopoxvirus causes umbilicated vesicles and lymphadenopathy, and is a consideration in an immunocompromised patient given recent outbreaks.
Orf (Ecthyma contagiosum)
This is a zoonotic parapoxvirus infection from sheep/goats that can cause umbilicated lesions in humans.
Milker's nodule
This is a zoonotic parapoxvirus infection from cattle that causes skin lesions similar to orf.
Vaccinia virus infection
This orthopoxvirus can cause umbilicated vesicles following vaccination or accidental exposure.
eliminated: Disseminated cryptococcosis
This fungal infection can cause umbilicated skin lesions in HIV patients but is ruled out by the confirmed viral etiology.
Herpes simplex virus infection
This is ruled out as the biopsy showed intracytoplasmic inclusions and poxvirus particles, not the characteristic intranuclear inclusions and multinucleated giant cells of herpesviruses.
Varicella-zoster virus infection
This is ruled out as the histopathology and electron microscopy findings are specific to a poxvirus, not a herpesvirus.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The presence of vesicles instead of papules argues against Poxvirus, which typically presents with papules or nodules.
